title: Life in the UK
variant_label: Life in the UK Real-Spec Practice
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public Life in the UK handbook and test syllabus. Not a capture of past exam questions.
source_label: Life in the UK practice bank

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: Which set of principles does the Life in the UK handbook describe as the fundamental values on which British society is based?
options: Democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
Monarchy, aristocracy, an established religion, and obedience to authority
Military service, national pride, economic growth, and a fixed social hierarchy
Free trade, private property, low taxation, and a minimal state
items.explanation: The handbook lists democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs as the fundamental principles, alongside participation in community life.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: At a citizenship ceremony a new citizen makes a pledge. What does that pledge commit the citizen to do?
options: Serve in the armed forces for a fixed period after becoming a citizen
Give loyalty to the United Kingdom, respect its rights and freedoms, uphold its democratic values, and observe its laws
Pay a higher rate of tax than other residents during the first year
Attend a place of worship at least once in every month
items.explanation: The citizenship pledge is a promise of loyalty to the United Kingdom to respect its rights and freedoms, uphold its democratic values, and observe its laws faithfully.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: As well as making the pledge, what else does an applicant normally do at a citizenship ceremony?
options: Sign a petition in support of the government
Join a political party of their own choosing
Take an oath or affirmation of allegiance to the monarch
Apply for a British passport on the spot
items.explanation: At the ceremony a new citizen swears an oath, or makes an affirmation, of allegiance to the monarch and then makes the pledge of loyalty to the United Kingdom.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: Which responsibility does the Life in the UK handbook list for everyone who lives in the United Kingdom?
options: Belonging to a recognised trade union
Serving on a jury at least once every year
Owning property in the local area
Obeying the law and respecting the rights of others
items.explanation: The handbook states that residents must obey the law, respect the rights of others, treat people fairly, look after themselves and their family, and care for the area in which they live.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: What does the principle of the rule of law mean in the United Kingdom?
options: The law applies to everyone, including the government and public officials
Only judges and magistrates are required to obey the law
The monarch may set aside any law of which the monarch disapproves
Laws apply only to citizens and never to visitors
items.explanation: The rule of law means that no one is above the law and that it applies equally to citizens, government and public officials alike.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: The handbook says that people in the United Kingdom should take part in their community. Which activity best illustrates that principle?
options: Paying income tax through an employer payroll
Volunteering to help a local charity or community group
Reading a national newspaper each day
Driving within the posted speed limit
items.explanation: Participation in community life, for example through volunteering or joining local groups and activities, is one of the values the handbook identifies for people living in the UK.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: Which item is named in the Life in the UK handbook as one of the fundamental principles of the United Kingdom?
options: Compulsory membership of a political party
A single state religion observed by all residents
Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
items.explanation: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is one of the fundamental principles, together with democracy, the rule of law and individual liberty.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: The handbook states that residents should treat others with fairness and respect. Which behaviour best reflects that responsibility?
options: Reporting neighbours to the authorities over minor disagreements
Insisting that everyone in the area follows the same customs
Buying goods only from businesses in the immediate locality
Treating people fairly and not discriminating against them because of their background
items.explanation: The values section asks residents to treat others with fairness and respect and not to discriminate against people because of their background or beliefs.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: A new citizen promises to fulfil their duties and obligations. According to the handbook, which of these is such an obligation?
options: Looking after yourself and your family and the area where you live
Donating a fixed sum of money to the government each year
Learning to speak a second language within a year of arrival
Joining the armed forces if the government asks
items.explanation: The handbook sets out responsibilities that include looking after yourself and your family and taking care of the area in which you live.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: Where does a successful applicant normally make the pledge and the oath or affirmation of allegiance?
options: At a polling station on election day
At a citizenship ceremony organised by the local authority
At a police station in the applicant's home town
At a bank when opening a United Kingdom account
items.explanation: New citizens attend a citizenship ceremony, arranged by the local authority, at which they make the oath or affirmation of allegiance and the pledge of loyalty.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: What does the principle of individual liberty mean for people living in the United Kingdom?
options: They may ignore any law with which they personally disagree
They may avoid paying taxes they consider unfair
They are free to live their lives as they choose within the limits of the law
They may use public services without contributing towards them
items.explanation: Individual liberty means people are free to make their own choices and live their lives as they wish, provided they act within the law.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.domain: The Values and Principles of the UK
items.stem: Which statement reflects how the handbook describes the values of the United Kingdom?
options: They are optional principles that each resident may accept or ignore
They apply only to people who hold British citizenship
They are enforced only during the period of a national election
They apply to everyone in the United Kingdom and rest on democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and tolerance
items.explanation: The values described in the handbook apply to everyone living in the United Kingdom, whether or not they are citizens, and are based on shared fundamental principles.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - The Values and Principles of the UK

items.stem: Which countries make up the United Kingdom?
options: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Scotland, Ireland and the Isle of Man
Great Britain, the Republic of Ireland and the Channel Islands
items.explanation: The United Kingdom is made up of four countries, namely England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and it is governed from Westminster.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which name is used for England, Scotland and Wales considered together without Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: Great Britain is the geographical term for England, Scotland and Wales, whereas the United Kingdom also includes Northern Ireland.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which term describes the group of islands that includes the United Kingdom, the Republic of Ireland and many smaller islands?
items.explanation: The British Isles is a geographical term for the group of islands that includes the United Kingdom, the Republic of Ireland and a number of smaller islands.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: What is the capital city of Wales?
items.explanation: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales and is the home of the Welsh Parliament, known as the Senedd.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: Belfast is the capital city of Northern Ireland and is the seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: What is the capital city of Scotland?
items.explanation: Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and is where the Scottish Parliament meets at Holyrood.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which statement about the role of the monarch in the United Kingdom is correct?
options: The monarch personally writes and passes all new laws
The monarch is elected by the members of Parliament
The monarch is the head of state and remains politically neutral
The monarch chooses the prime minister without regard to any convention
items.explanation: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy in which the monarch is the head of state, reigns rather than rules, and stays politically neutral.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Where is the Parliament of the United Kingdom based?
items.explanation: The United Kingdom Parliament sits at Westminster in London, while the devolved bodies meet in Edinburgh, Belfast and Cardiff.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which of these is a Crown dependency rather than a part of the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: The Isle of Man, together with the Channel Islands, is a Crown dependency and is not part of the United Kingdom.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: In which city does the Welsh Parliament, known as the Senedd, meet?
items.explanation: The Senedd, the Welsh Parliament, meets in Cardiff, which is also the capital city of Wales.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which patron saint is associated with Scotland and is celebrated on 30 November?
items.explanation: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland and St Andrew's Day is celebrated on 30 November each year.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: Which national emblem is traditionally associated with Wales?
items.explanation: The daffodil, along with the leek, is a national emblem of Wales, while the rose, thistle and shamrock represent England, Scotland and Northern Ireland respectively.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - What is the UK

items.stem: In which year did the Roman Emperor Claudius begin the conquest of Britain?
items.explanation: The Roman conquest of Britain began in 43 AD under the Emperor Claudius, and the Romans remained until around 410 AD.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: For what purpose did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall?
options: To mark the boundary between England and Wales
To defend the northern frontier of their province against the Picts
To carry water to the growing city of London
To provide a road for their legions to reach Ireland
items.explanation: Hadrian's Wall was built to protect the northern frontier of the Roman province of Britannia against attacks by the Picts.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which groups of Germanic peoples settled in Britain after the Romans left?
items.explanation: After the Romans departed, the Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled in Britain, and it is from the Angles that the name England is derived.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Who led the Norman invasion of England in 1066 and became king after the Battle of Hastings?
items.explanation: William the Conqueror defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became the first Norman king of England.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which document, agreed by King John in 1215, limited the powers of the monarch?
items.explanation: Magna Carta, sealed by King John in 1215, established that even the monarch was subject to the law and limited royal power.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which king broke with the Roman Catholic Church and established the Church of England?
items.explanation: Henry VIII broke away from the Roman Catholic Church and made himself head of the new Church of England during the Reformation.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated during the reign of Elizabeth I?
items.explanation: The Spanish Armada, sent to invade England, was defeated in 1588 during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Who was the leading figure in the plot to blow up the Houses of Parliament in 1605?
items.explanation: Guy Fawkes was the most famous member of the group that plotted in 1605 to blow up the Houses of Parliament, an event remembered as the Gunpowder Plot.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: What happened to King Charles I at the end of the English Civil War?
options: He abdicated in favour of his son
He fled to France and never returned
He was restored to the throne in 1660
items.explanation: King Charles I was defeated in the Civil War and executed in 1649, and the monarchy was restored under Charles II only in 1660.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which event of 1688 led to the Bill of Rights being agreed the following year?
items.explanation: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced James II with William and Mary, and the Bill of Rights of 1689 confirmed the powers of Parliament over the monarch.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: What did the Act of Union of 1707 create?
options: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The Kingdom of Great Britain by uniting England and Scotland
items.explanation: The Act of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain, with a single Parliament at Westminster.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which engineer is credited with major improvements to the steam engine that helped to drive the Industrial Revolution?
items.explanation: James Watt made major improvements to the steam engine, while George Stephenson is associated with the development of the railway locomotive.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which British admiral died at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
items.explanation: Admiral Horatio Nelson died at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, a decisive naval victory over the French and Spanish fleets.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Who commanded the British and allied forces that defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
items.explanation: The Duke of Wellington commanded the allied forces that defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: During which years did the First World War take place?
items.explanation: The First World War was fought from 1914 to 1918, while the Second World War took place from 1939 to 1945.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Who was the prime minister of the United Kingdom for most of the Second World War?
items.explanation: Winston Churchill became prime minister in 1940 and led the United Kingdom for most of the Second World War.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: In which year was the National Health Service established?
items.explanation: The National Health Service was founded in 1948 to provide healthcare funded by taxation and free at the point of use.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: In which year did the United Kingdom join the European Economic Community, then known as the Common Market?
items.explanation: The United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community, the Common Market, in 1973, several years after its first application was refused.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Long and Illustrious History

items.stem: Which church is the established Christian church in England?
items.explanation: The Church of England is the established church in England, while the Church of Scotland is the national church in Scotland.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which language has official status in Wales alongside English?
items.explanation: Welsh has official status in Wales, while Scottish Gaelic, Ulster Scots and Cornish are among the other regional languages of the United Kingdom.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which festival, celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, is widely known as the festival of lights?
items.explanation: Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, while Eid is a Muslim festival and Hanukkah is a Jewish one.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which sport is associated with the Wimbledon championships held each summer?
items.explanation: Wimbledon is the world's oldest tennis tournament and is held in London each summer.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: At which Scottish town is the sport of golf traditionally said to have originated?
items.explanation: Golf is traditionally said to have originated at St Andrews in Scotland, which remains famous for its historic golf course.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which public holiday is observed in Scotland but not in England?
items.explanation: Scotland observes an additional public holiday on 2 January, whereas England and Wales do not treat that date as a bank holiday.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which public holiday is celebrated in Northern Ireland on 17 March?
items.explanation: St Patrick's Day is celebrated on 17 March and is a public holiday in Northern Ireland, while Orangemen's Day falls on 12 July.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: What is the minimum age at which a person may vote in a United Kingdom general election?
items.explanation: The minimum voting age in a United Kingdom general election is 18, though some devolved elections allow voting from a younger age.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: At what age may a person in the United Kingdom normally obtain a licence to drive a car?
items.explanation: A person may normally apply for a licence to drive a car in the United Kingdom from the age of 17.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: At what age may a person legally buy alcohol in the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: In the United Kingdom a person must be 18 to buy alcohol, although some exceptions apply to accompanying meals in licensed premises.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: What is the official currency of the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: The currency of the United Kingdom is the pound sterling, which is issued and managed with the Bank of England.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which public body provides healthcare that is free at the point of use for residents of the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: The National Health Service provides healthcare that is largely free at the point of use and is funded through general taxation.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which national broadcaster is funded mainly by a television licence fee paid by households?
items.explanation: The British Broadcasting Corporation, the BBC, is funded principally by the television licence fee rather than by advertising.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which payments are deducted from earnings to help fund public services in the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: People in work pay income tax and National Insurance contributions, which help to fund public services such as the health service.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which law makes it illegal to discriminate against people because of characteristics such as age, disability, race or religion?
items.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 brought together earlier anti-discrimination laws and protects people from unfair treatment because of protected characteristics.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which national charity cares for historic places and areas of countryside in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: The National Trust is a charity that looks after historic buildings and countryside, while the National Trust for Scotland performs a similar role there.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: Which sport is played at Lord's and features the Ashes series contested between England and Australia?
items.explanation: Cricket is played at Lord's in London, and the Ashes is the long-standing Test series between England and Australia.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society

items.stem: How often is a national census normally carried out in the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: A national census is normally held every ten years to gather information about the population and how people live.
items.reference: Life in the UK Handbook - A Modern, Thriving Society
